section: CONSTITUTION OF OILS AND FATS, AND THEIR SAPONIFICATION.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what mixed glyceride did Holde and Stange report in olive oil, and in what proportion?
reference_answer: Holde and Stange reported oleodidaturin in olive oil at from 1 to 2 per cent.
required_key_points: oleodidaturin
from 1 to 2 per cent.
supporting_passage:
Hansen has since found that tallow contains oleodipalmitin,
from C_{3}H_{5}(OC_{18}H_{35}O)(OC_{16}H_{31}O), stearodipalmitin,
C_{3}H_{5}(OC_{18}H_{35}O)(OC_{16}H_{31}O), oleopalmitostearin,
C_{3}H_{5}(OC_{18}H_{33}O)(OC_{16}H_{31}O)(OC_{18}H_{35}O) and
palmitodistearin, CH(OC_{16}H_{31}O)(OC_{18}H_{35}O)_{2}, the latter of
which has also been obtained by Kreis and Hafner from lard, while Holde
and Stange have shown that olive oil contains from 1 to 2 per cent. of
oleodidaturin, C_{3}H_{5}(OC_{18}H_{33}O)(OC_{17}H_{33}O)_{2}, and
Hehner and Mitchell have obtained indications of mixed glycerides in
linseed oil (which they consider contains a compound of glycerol with
two radicles of linolenic acid and one radicle of oleic acid), also in
cod-liver, cod, whale and shark oils.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what acids did the authors identify in the material formerly classified as margaric acid?
reference_answer: They identified margaric acid as a mixture of stearic, palmitic and oleic acids.
required_key_points: stearic, palmitic and oleic acids
supporting_passage:
Medullic and margaric acids, which were formerly included in this
series, have now been shown to consist of mixtures of stearic and
palmitic, and stearic palmitic and oleic acids respectively.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what operating conditions and result did De Wilde and Reychler report for treating oleic acid in autoclaves?
reference_answer: They heated oleic acid with 1 per cent. of iodine to 270 deg.-280 deg. C. in autoclaves, converting about 70 per cent. into stearic acid.
required_key_points: 1 per cent. of iodine
270 deg.-280 deg. C.
about 70 per cent. converted into stearic acid
supporting_passage:
De Wilde and Reychler have shown that by heating oleic acid with 1 per
cent. of iodine in autoclaves up to 270 deg.-280 deg. C., about 70 per cent. is
converted into stearic acid, and Zuerer has devised (German Patent
62,407) a process whereby the oleic acid is first converted by the
action of chlorine into the dichloride, which is then reduced with
nascent hydrogen.

section: I. Application of Heat or Electricity.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how did Mannig introduce steam in his process to limit fatty-acid discoloration, and at what pressure?
reference_answer: Mannig projected steam at 8 to 10 atmospheres against a baffle plate in a closed vessel so it mixed with the fat or oil as a spray.
required_key_points: 8 to 10 atmospheres
steam projected against a baffle plate in a closed vessel to mix with fat or oil as a spray
supporting_passage:
To
expose the acids to heat for a minimum of time, and so prevent
discoloration, Mannig has patented (Germ. Pat. 160,111) a process
whereby steam under a pressure of 8 to 10 atmospheres is projected
against a baffle plate mounted in a closed vessel, where it mixes with
the fat or oil in the form of a spray, the rate of hydrolysis being
thereby, it is claimed, much increased.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what relative quantities of Linaria and castor seeds did Fokin find to have equal fat-splitting activity?
reference_answer: Fokin found that twenty to thirty parts of Linaria had the same lipolytic activity as four to five parts of castor seeds.
required_key_points: twenty to thirty parts of Linaria
four to five parts of castor seeds
supporting_passage:
The seeds of _Chelidonium majus_ were found to have as
great, and possibly greater, enzymic activity than castor seeds, but
those of _Linaria_ are much weaker, twenty to thirty parts having only
the same lipolytic activity as four to five parts of castor seeds.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what treatment followed the incubation of Connstein's industrial castor-seed emulsion to separate the fatty acids?
reference_answer: The mixture was heated to 70 deg.-80 deg. C. and treated with a 25 per cent. sulphuric acid solution amounting to one-fiftieth of the fat originally used.
required_key_points: temperature raised to 70 deg.-80 deg. C.
25 per cent. solution of sulphuric acid
one-fiftieth of the total quantity of fat originally taken
supporting_passage:
The temperature is then raised to 70 deg.-80 deg. C.,
which destroys the enzyme, and a 25 per cent. solution of sulphuric
acid, equal in amount to one-fiftieth of the total quantity of fat
originally taken, added to promote separation of the fatty acids.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what method did Lombard prescribe for preparing a liquid to replace water in enzymic fat splitting?
reference_answer: Lombard proposed triturating oil cake with its own weight of water, allowing spontaneous proteolytic hydrolysis at 40 deg. C. for eight days, then filtering and using the filtrate instead of water.
required_key_points: triturate oil cake with its own weight of water
spontaneous proteolytic hydrolysis at 40 deg. C. for eight days
filter and use the filtrate in place of water
supporting_passage:
Lombard (Fr. Pat. 350,179, 1904) claims that acids act as stimulating
agents in the enzymic hydrolysis of oils, and further that a simple
method of obtaining the active product is to triturate oil cake with its
own weight of water, allow the mixture to undergo spontaneous
proteolytic hydrolysis at 40 deg. C. for eight days, and then filter, the
filtrate obtained being used in place of water in the enzymic process.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what maximum fatty-acid yields did experiments with steapsin give from cotton-seed oil and lard after fifty-six days?
reference_answer: Steapsin liberated 83-86 per cent. of fatty acids from cotton-seed oil, compared with 46 per cent. from lard in the same time.
required_key_points: 83-86 per cent. from cotton-seed oil
46 per cent. from lard
supporting_passage:
The former, although it has
been shown by Kastle and Loevenhart (_Amer. Chem. Journ._, 1900, 49) to
readily hydrolyse ethyl butyrate, is found to have very little
fat-splitting power, but with steapsin more favourable results have been
obtained, though the yield of fatty acids in this case is considerably
inferior to that given by castor seeds. With cotton-seed oil, 83-86 per
cent. of fatty acids were liberated as a maximum after fifty-six days,
but with lard only 46 per cent. were produced in the same time.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what observable characteristics did Rahn report for the unidentified bacillus that decomposed oleic acid?
reference_answer: The bacillus was motile and produced a green fluorescent colouring matter.
required_key_points: motile
produced a green fluorescent colouring matter
supporting_passage:
A motile bacillus, producing
a green fluorescent colouring matter, but not identified, had a marked
hydrolytic action and decomposed oleic acid.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what sequence did Dreymann prescribe in his second patented method for treating fatty acids?
reference_answer: Dreymann proposed making methyl esters using methyl alcohol and hydrochloric acid gas, purifying the esters by steam distillation, and then decomposing them with superheated steam in an autoclave.
required_key_points: convert fatty acids to methyl esters with methyl alcohol and hydrochloric acid gas
purify the esters by steam distillation
decompose the purified esters with superheated steam in an autoclave
supporting_passage:
The second method claimed consists in the conversion of the fatty acids
into their methyl esters by treatment with methyl alcohol and
hydrochloric acid gas, and purification of the esters by steam
distillation, the pure esters being subsequently decomposed with
superheated steam, in an autoclave, with or without the addition of an
oxide, _e.g._, 0.1 per cent. zinc oxide, to facilitate their
decomposition.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how did the recommended amount of Twitchell's reagent differ between good-quality and lower-grade starting material?
reference_answer: For good material, from 1/2 to 3/4 per cent. was sufficient; for lower-grade material, proportionately more was needed, up to 2 per cent.
required_key_points: good material: from 1/2 to 3/4 per cent.
lower-grade material: up to 2 per cent.
supporting_passage:
The amount of reagent used varies with
the grade of material, the smaller the amount consistent with efficient
results, the better the colour of the finished product; with good
material, from 1/2 to 3/4 per cent. is sufficient, but for materials of
lower grade proportionately more up to 2 per cent. is required.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what explanation did the authors give for castor oil's unusually limited hydrolysis during Lewkowitsch's hydrochloric-acid treatment?
reference_answer: They attributed it to the different constitution of castor oil’s fatty acids and the ready formation of polymerisation products.
required_key_points: different constitution of its fatty acids
ready formation of polymerisation products
supporting_passage:
Castor oil is abnormal in only
undergoing about 20 per cent. hydrolysis, but this is attributed to the
different constitution of its fatty acids, and the ready formation of
polymerisation products.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what proportion of zinc oxide did Poullain and Michaud recommend in their patented process for saponifying oils and fats?
reference_answer: They recommended adding 0.2 to 0.5 per cent. of zinc oxide to the oil or fat.
required_key_points: 0.2 to 0.5 per cent.
supporting_passage:
Poullain and Michaud, in 1882, were
granted a patent for this process, the quantity of zinc oxide
recommended to be added to the oil or fat being 0.2 to 0.5 per cent.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what solidification temperatures did the authors report for stearin cooled after heating to 76 deg. C. versus 71.6 deg. C.?
reference_answer: After being heated to 76 deg. C., stearin solidifies at 55 deg. C.; after heating to 71.6 deg. C., it solidifies at 70 deg. C.
required_key_points: 55 deg. C. for the first heating condition
70 deg. C. for the second heating condition
supporting_passage:
If this liquid be further heated to 76 deg.
C., and allowed to cool, it will not solidify until 55 deg. C. is reached,
but if the liquid at 71.6 deg. C. be allowed to cool, solidification will
occur at 70 deg. C.

section: Hydrolysis or Saponification of Oils and Fats.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what molecularity did Fanto assign to the saponification of olive oil with caustic potash in homogeneous solution?
reference_answer: Fanto concluded that saponification under these conditions was practically quadrimolecular.
required_key_points: practically quadrimolecular
supporting_passage:
Balbiano and
Marcusson doubt the validity of Lewkowitsch's conclusions, and Fanto,
experimenting on the saponification of olive oil with caustic potash, is
unable to detect the intermediate formation of any mono- or diglyceride,
and concludes that in homogeneous solution the saponification is
practically quadrimolecular.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, under what condition did Nicloux say the activity of his castor-seed substance called 'lipaseidine' would be destroyed?
reference_answer: Nicloux said that contact with water in the absence of oil destroyed its activity.
required_key_points: contact with water in the absence of oil
supporting_passage:
This active substance, which he terms "lipaseidine," is
considered to be not an enzyme, though it acts as such, following the
ordinary laws of enzyme action; its activity is destroyed by contact
with water in the absence of oil.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what fatty-acid yield and steaming duration did Lewkowitsch report for tallow treated with 98 per cent. sulphuric acid?
reference_answer: The 98 per cent. acid produced 93 per cent. of fatty acids after nine hours' steaming.
required_key_points: 93 per cent. of fatty acids
nine hours' steaming
supporting_passage:
Using 98 per cent. acid, 93 per cent. of fatty
acids were obtained after nine hours' steaming, and after another seven
hours, only 0.6 per cent. more fatty acids were produced.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how did the lime requirement for saponification in an open vessel at 100 deg.-105 deg. C. compare with that in pressurised autoclaves?
reference_answer: In an open vessel, an excess of 3-5 per cent. above the theoretical quantity of lime was required; in pressurised autoclaves, 2-3 per cent. on the fat sufficed for almost perfect hydrolysis.
required_key_points: open vessel: an excess of 3-5 per cent. above the theoretical quantity of lime
pressurised autoclaves: 2-3 per cent. on the fat
supporting_passage:
It is found in practice, however, that an excess of
3-5 per cent. above the theoretical quantity of lime is necessary to
complete the hydrolysis of a fat when carried on in an open vessel at
100 deg.-105 deg. C., but that if the saponification be conducted under
pressure in autoclaves the amount of lime necessary to secure almost
perfect hydrolysis is reduced to 2-3 per cent. on the fat, the treatment
of fats with 3 per cent. of lime under a pressure of 10 atmospheres
producing a yield of 95 per cent. of fatty acids in seven hours.
